definition: Proximal gradient (forward backward splitting) methods for learning is an area of research in optimization and statistical learning theory which studies algorithms for a general class of convex regularization problems where the regularization penalty may not be differentiable.
details: One such example is ℓ 1 {\displaystyle \ell _{1}} regularization (also known as Lasso) of the form min w ∈ R d 1 n ∑ i = 1 n ( y i − ⟨ w , x i ⟩ ) 2 + λ ‖ w ‖ 1 , where x i ∈ R d and y i ∈ R . {\displaystyle \min _{w\in \mathbb {R} ^{d}}{\frac {1}{n}}\sum _{i=1}^{n}(y_{i}-\langle w,x_{i}\rangle )^{2}+\lambda \|w\|_{1},\quad {\text{ where }}x_{i}\in \mathbb {R} ^{d}{\text{ and }}y_{i}\in \mathbb {R} .} Proximal gradient methods offer a general framework for solving regularization problems from statistical learning theory with penalties that are tailored to a specific problem application. Such customized penalties can help to induce certain structure in problem solutions, such as sparsity (in the case of lasso) or group structure (in the case of group lasso).

explainer.lead: This family of optimisation algorithms handles convex learning problems whose regulariser is not differentiable, which broadens what can be trained.

tiers.eli5: When a penalty has sharp corners you can't just slide downhill, so you take a normal step and then snap back to the nearest sensible point.
tiers.practitioner: They are used to fit sparse models like Lasso by alternating a gradient step with a proximal step; a pitfall is choosing a step size that makes the iteration unstable or slow.
tiers.paperLevel: For problems such as minimising (1/n) sum over i of (y_i minus inner product of w and x_i) squared plus lambda times the L1 norm of w, the method alternates a gradient step with a proximal operator; convergence guarantees assume convexity.

explainer.example: Fitting a Lasso regression by taking a gradient step on the squared loss and then applying soft-thresholding, the proximal operator of the L1 penalty, to shrink weights to zero.
